kettle.motion.title: Convection and boiling
captions: Heated water expands and gets lighter, so it rises in the middle and sinks at the sides.
Hot spots at the bottom let vapour bubbles form (nucleation), then they rise and burst.
At 100 °C extra energy goes into turning water to vapour, not heating it. That is latent heat.

kettle.cutaway.title: Cut open
captions: Under the floor of the jug sits the heating element: a coil of wire that gets hot when current flows.
Water touching the hot floor warms, rises up the middle, cools at the top and sinks at the sides.
When it boils, steam runs down a tube to a metal strip in the base. The strip bends and clicks the power off.

kettle.whatif.title: What if
captions: Boiling time grows almost in a straight line with the water. Twice the water needs about twice the time and energy.
Water that starts at 60 °C needs only half the heating, so it boils in half the time.

kettle.flow.title: Follow the energy
captions: Electricity flows from the socket into a coil of wire in the base: the heating element.
The element resists the current, so all of the electrical energy turns into heat, which passes into the water.
About 88 percent ends up in the water. The rest warms the jug and the air around it.
At 100 °C the water turns to steam. The steam heats a metal strip that bends and clicks the kettle off.

kettle.number.title: The number
captions: Heating one litre of water by 80 degrees takes 335 kilojoules. From the socket that is about 0.11 kWh.
A 2 kW kettle needs about three minutes for it, and it costs about two cents.
The same energy would light a 10 watt LED lamp for more than ten hours. Boil only what you need.
